title: Basic Microsoft Excel
tagline: From first cell to a finished report, with practice in every module
summary: Learn spreadsheets the practical way: enter data, write formulas, summarise, decide with IF, sort and filter, and finish with a chart. Every module has a working spreadsheet lab that checks your work.

modules.title: Meet the workbook
modules.summary: How a spreadsheet is laid out, how to type data into it and how to make it easy to read.
modules.outcome: You can find any cell by its address, enter text, numbers and dates correctly and format a small table so others can read it.
modules.intro: Spreadsheets are the most used business tool in the world. Accountants, teachers, shop owners and engineers all keep their numbers in a grid. In this module you learn how the grid is organised, how to type into it without making the mistakes that cause trouble later, and how to make a sheet clear to read.

topics.title: Workbooks, worksheets and cells
topics.html:
A spreadsheet file is called a workbook. Inside it are one or more worksheets (the tabs at the bottom). Each worksheet is a huge grid. The columns are named with letters (A, B, C ...) and the rows with numbers (1, 2, 3 ...).

Definition

Cell. One box in the grid, found where a column meets a row. Its name is its address: the column letter first, then the row number, such as B3.

Reading cell addresses
AddressWhere it is
A1Column A, row 1: the top-left cell
C5Column C, row 5
B2:B6A range: the cells from B2 down to B6
A1:C3A range of 9 cells: three columns by three rows

When you click a cell it becomes the active cell. Its address shows in the Name box, and what you typed shows in the formula bar. Both are worth watching: the cell may display 6 while the formula bar shows =B2+B3.

Tip

Always say addresses the same way: column first, then row. B3 is not the same cell as C2.

Check what you just learned

1. What is the address of the cell in column D, row 7?
  • D7 (correct)
  • 7D
  • D:7
  • R7C4

The column letter comes first, then the row number: D7.

2. What does B2:B6 mean?
  • Only cells B2 and B6
  • A range of five cells from B2 down to B6 (correct)
  • The sum of B2 and B6
  • Row 2 and row 6

A colon joins the first and last cell of a range, and everything between them is included.

3. Where can you see the real formula that a cell contains?
  • In the cell itself always
  • In the tab name
  • In the formula bar (correct)
  • In the row number

The cell shows the result, the formula bar shows what was typed.
keyPoints: A workbook holds worksheets; a worksheet is a grid of cells.
A cell address is column letter then row number, such as C5.
A range such as B2:B6 means a block of cells.
The formula bar shows what is really in the cell.

topics.title: Entering and editing data
topics.html:
Click a cell and type. Press Enter to confirm and move down, Tab to confirm and move right, or Esc to cancel. To change something later, select the cell and press F2, or double-click.

A spreadsheet decides what you typed. Text (names, labels) lines up on the left. Numbers line up on the right. If a number sits on the left, it was probably typed with a space or a letter in it and is being treated as text, and formulas will ignore it.

Types of data

  • Text: Priya, Nov sales, Item
  • Numbers: 450, 12.5, 18%
  • Dates: 14/03/2026 (stored as numbers, shown as dates)
  • Formulas: anything starting with =
Watch out

Never type a unit inside a number cell. Type 250 and put the unit in the heading (Price in rupees). A cell holding 250 rs is text, and =SUM() will skip it.

Tip

Made a mistake? Undo with Ctrl+Z (Cmd+Z on a Mac). Redo with Ctrl+Y. You can undo many steps.

Common mistakes

  • Typing numbers with a space or a letter, which turns them into text.
  • Leaving blank rows in the middle of a table, which later breaks sorting and charts.
  • Putting two kinds of information in one column.

Check what you just learned

1. A number you typed sits on the left of its cell. What is the most likely reason?
  • Excel is broken
  • It is a date
  • The column is too narrow
  • It was typed with extra characters and is stored as text (correct)

Numbers align right by default. A left-aligned number has been read as text.

2. Which key cancels what you are typing in a cell?
  • Esc (correct)
  • F2
  • Tab
  • Enter

Esc cancels the entry and keeps the old content.
keyPoints: Enter moves down, Tab moves right, Esc cancels, F2 edits.
Numbers align right, text aligns left; left-aligned numbers are a warning sign.
Keep one kind of data in each column and no blank rows.

topics.title: Making a sheet readable
topics.html:
A sheet other people can read quickly is worth much more than a clever one. Four habits do most of the work.

Four habits of a readable sheet

  1. Make the heading row bold so it stands apart from the data.
  2. Widen columns until nothing is cut off.
  3. Use number formats: currency for money, percent for rates, fixed decimals for measurements.
  4. Use colour sparingly, to mark totals or inputs, never as decoration.
Number formats change the look, not the value
You typeFormatIt shows
0.18Percent18%
1250Currency₹1,250.00
3.141592 decimals3.14
1250.6Whole number1251
Tip

A number format never changes the value underneath. 3.14159 shown as 3.14 is still 3.14159 when used in a formula.

Check what you just learned

1. You format 0.18 as Percent. What is stored in the cell?
  • 18
  • 0.18 (correct)
  • 1800
  • Text

Formatting changes only the display. The value stays 0.18.

2. Which is the best use of colour?
  • Every row a different colour
  • Making all text red
  • Highlighting the totals (correct)
  • Colouring empty cells

Colour should guide the eye to what matters, such as totals.

Key terms: flip and sort

Workbook
The whole spreadsheet file
Worksheet
One grid inside a workbook (a tab)
Cell address
Column letter plus row number, such as B3
Range
A block of cells such as B2:B6
Active cell
The cell you have selected
Number format
How a number is displayed, without changing its value
keyPoints: Bold headings, wide columns, number formats and little colour.
Formats change appearance, not the stored value.

modules.title: Formulas that calculate
modules.summary: Write formulas with cell references, understand how they behave when copied and lock a cell with the dollar sign.
modules.outcome: You can write a formula that updates itself, explain the difference between relative and absolute references, and avoid the most common formula mistakes.
modules.intro: Typing results is not what spreadsheets are for. The power of Excel is that a formula remembers how to calculate, so when a number changes the answer changes with it. This module shows how to write formulas, how references behave and how to keep one cell fixed.

topics.title: Your first formula
topics.html:
Every formula starts with an equals sign. After it you write the calculation using numbers, operators and cell addresses. The cell shows the answer; the formula bar keeps the formula.

The arithmetic operators
OperatorMeaningExampleResult
+Add=5+38
-Subtract=5-32
*Multiply=5*315
/Divide=15/35
^Power=2^38
%Percent=200*10%20

Always point at cells, not at typed numbers. With =B2*C2 the answer changes when the quantity in B2 changes. With =4*45 it never will.

Worked example

Why references beat typed numbers

Notebooks cost ₹45. Asha buys 4, so you type =4*45 and get 180. The next day she buys 6.

  1. With =4*45 you must find the formula and edit it.
  2. With =B2*C2 you only change B2 from 4 to 6.
  3. The answer updates itself to 270.

Answer. Use cell references in formulas so a change in the data changes the answer automatically.

Excel follows the usual order of operations: brackets first, then powers, then multiplication and division, then addition and subtraction. Brackets make your intention clear.

Tip

=2+3*4 gives 14, because multiplication goes first. =(2+3)*4 gives 20.

Check what you just learned

1. What must every formula start with?
  • A letter
  • A dollar sign
  • A bracket
  • An equals sign (correct)

The equals sign tells the sheet to calculate.

2. What does =2+3*4 give?
  • 14 (correct)
  • 20
  • 24
  • 9

Multiplication goes first: 3×4 is 12, plus 2 is 14.

3. Why is =B2*C2 better than =4*45?
  • It is shorter
  • It updates when B2 or C2 change (correct)
  • It is faster
  • It avoids brackets

References follow the data.
keyPoints: A formula starts with =.
Use cell references, not typed numbers.
Brackets, powers, then × ÷, then + − is the order of working.

topics.title: Copying formulas: relative references
topics.html:
A reference like B2 is relative: it means 'the cell in column B, in this row'. When you copy a formula down one row, Excel shifts the reference down with it. That is why one formula can fill a whole column.

What happens when =B2*C2 is copied down
Copied toFormula becomes
D2 (original)=B2*C2
D3=B3*C3
D4=B4*C4
D5=B5*C5

The reference moved because it describes a position relative to the formula: 'two columns left of me'. Copy the same formula one column right and the references shift one column right as well.

Common mistakes

  • Typing each formula by hand instead of copying: slow and easy to get wrong.
  • Copying a formula that points at a fixed cell (such as a tax rate) without locking it; see the next lesson.

Check what you just learned

1. D2 holds =B2*C2. What does D4 hold after copying D2 down?
  • =B2*C2
  • =D4
  • =B4*C4 (correct)
  • =B3*C3

Each step down moves both references down by one row.

2. What does a relative reference describe?
  • A fixed cell
  • A page
  • A colour
  • A position relative to the formula's cell (correct)

It points at a cell by its distance from the formula.
keyPoints: A relative reference moves when the formula is copied.
Copying one formula down a column is how a whole column is calculated.

topics.title: Absolute references and the dollar sign
topics.html:
Sometimes a formula must keep pointing at the same cell however it is copied: a tax rate, a target, an exchange rate. Put a dollar sign before the column letter and the row number to lock them: $B$1.

Relative, absolute and mixed
WrittenBehaviour when copied
B1Relative: column and row both move
$B$1Absolute: nothing moves
$B1Mixed: column fixed, row moves
B$1Mixed: column moves, row fixed
Worked example

A price list with tax

The tax rate 18% is in B1. Prices are in B4:B6. You want tax in C4:C6.

  1. In C4 write =B4*$B$1.
  2. Copy C4 down to C5 and C6.
  3. C5 becomes =B5*$B$1 and C6 becomes =B6*$B$1: the price moves, the rate stays.

Answer. Lock the rate with $B$1 so every row uses the same tax cell. Change B1 once and the whole sheet updates.

Change the rate once, everything updates

Move the tax rate and the price and watch the results change.

Adjust Price (rupees), Tax rate (%) and see Tax, Price with tax change.

Tip

In Excel you can press F4 while typing a reference to add the dollar signs for you.

Watch out

If you forget the dollar signs the rate reference slides down to B2, B3 ... which are empty or hold prices, and the answers become wrong or show zero.

Check what you just learned

1. What does $B$1 mean?
  • Always cell B1, even when copied (correct)
  • A price in dollars
  • Two cells
  • A mistake

The dollar signs lock the column and the row.

2. A formula =B4*B1 is copied down to row 5. What does it become?
  • =B5*B1
  • =B5*B2 (correct)
  • =B4*B2
  • =B5*$B$1

Both references are relative, so both move down: the rate reference slips to B2, a classic mistake.

Key terms: flip and sort

Formula
A calculation that starts with =
Operator
A symbol such as + - * / ^
Relative reference
Moves when the formula is copied
Absolute reference
Locked with dollar signs, never moves
Order of operations
Brackets, powers, × ÷, then + −
keyPoints: $B$1 is locked and never moves when copied.
Lock cells that hold a rate or target that many formulas share.
F4 adds the dollar signs while typing.

modules.title: Functions that summarise
modules.summary: Use SUM, AVERAGE, MIN, MAX and COUNT, and choose the right one for a task.
modules.outcome: You can summarise a column of numbers in seconds and avoid the common range mistakes.
modules.intro: A function is a ready-made formula with a name. Instead of writing B2+B3+B4+B5+B6+B7 you write =SUM(B2:B7). Functions save time and avoid slips, and a few of them cover most everyday work.

topics.title: SUM, AVERAGE, MIN, MAX and COUNT
topics.html:
Every function has a name, then brackets, and inside the brackets the arguments (what it works on). Most take a range such as B2:B7.

The five everyday functions
FunctionWhat it doesExample
SUMAdds the numbers=SUM(B2:B7)
AVERAGETotal divided by how many=AVERAGE(B2:B7)
MAXThe biggest number=MAX(B2:B7)
MINThe smallest number=MIN(B2:B7)
COUNTHow many cells hold numbers=COUNT(B2:B7)
Worked example

A class's marks

Marks in B2:B7 are 78, 92, 64, 85, 71 and 90.

  1. SUM gives 480.
  2. AVERAGE gives 480 / 6 = 80.
  3. MAX gives 92 and MIN gives 64.
  4. COUNT gives 6.

Answer. Total 480, average 80, highest 92, lowest 64, six marks.

Tip

You can click and drag over cells while typing a function to fill in the range, instead of typing it.

Check what you just learned

1. Which function finds the largest number in a range?
  • SUM
  • COUNT
  • MAX (correct)
  • MIN

MAX returns the biggest number.

2. Marks of 10, 20 and 30 are in a range. What does AVERAGE give?
  • 60
  • 10
  • 30
  • 20 (correct)

60 divided by 3 is 20.
keyPoints: A function has a name, brackets and arguments.
SUM, AVERAGE, MAX, MIN and COUNT summarise a range.
Ranges such as B2:B7 cover every cell between the two ends.

topics.title: Ranges, blanks and text
topics.html:
Summary functions look only at numbers inside a range. They quietly skip empty cells and text. That is usually what you want, but it hides two traps.

Two traps to watch for

  • A number stored as text (for example 85 marks) is skipped, so the total is too small.
  • A range that stops one row early leaves the last value out.
Worked example

The missing last row

Sales are in B2:B8 but the formula says =SUM(B2:B7).

  1. The total leaves out B8.
  2. Nothing shows an error, so nobody notices.
  3. Fix: extend the range to B2:B8, or select the whole column data.

Answer. A range that is too short gives a wrong answer without any warning, so always check the first and last cell of every range.

COUNT counts only cells holding numbers. If you need to count all filled cells including text, a related function does exactly that (COUNTA). Both help you check that no row was missed.

Tip

Check the total by eye: is it roughly the number of rows multiplied by a typical value?

Check what you just learned

1. Why might =SUM(B2:B9) give a total that is too low?
  • Some cells hold text instead of numbers (correct)
  • Excel rounds down
  • SUM only adds the first five
  • B column is hidden

Numbers stored as text are skipped.

2. How can you check that a range covers every row?
  • Hope for the best
  • Compare COUNT with the number of rows (correct)
  • Delete the formula
  • Change the font

COUNT shows how many numbers were found.
keyPoints: Summary functions skip text and blanks.
A short range gives a silent wrong answer.
COUNT helps confirm how many numbers were used.

topics.title: Rounding and tidy results
topics.html:
Averages often give long decimals such as 78.33333. Use ROUND to keep a neat result: =ROUND(AVERAGE(B2:B7),1) rounds the average to one decimal place.

Formula · ROUND

=ROUND(number, digits)

digits is how many places to keep. 0 means a whole number; 2 means two decimals.

Rounding examples
FormulaResult
=ROUND(78.3333,1)78.3
=ROUND(78.3333,0)78
=ROUND(1234.5678,2)1234.57
=ROUND(2.5,0)3
Watch out

A number format only changes how a value looks. ROUND changes the value itself. Use ROUND when a later formula must use the rounded number, such as an invoice total.

Check what you just learned

1. What does =ROUND(78.3333,1) give?
  • 78
  • 78.33
  • 78.3 (correct)
  • 80

One decimal place keeps 78.3.

2. When should you use ROUND instead of a number format?
  • When the look is all that matters
  • Only for dates
  • Never
  • When later formulas must use the rounded value (correct)

ROUND really changes the value.

Key terms: flip and sort

Function
A named, ready-made formula
Argument
What a function works on, inside the brackets
SUM
Adds numbers
AVERAGE
Total divided by the count
COUNT
Counts cells holding numbers
ROUND
Keeps a set number of decimals
keyPoints: ROUND(number, digits) keeps a set number of decimals.
ROUND changes the value; a number format changes only the look.

modules.title: Decisions and counting
modules.summary: Make a sheet decide with IF and count or total only the rows that meet a condition.
modules.outcome: You can write an IF formula, count matching rows with COUNTIF and total them with SUMIF.
modules.intro: So far every formula treated all rows the same. Real questions are about some rows: who passed, which region sold most, how many orders were late. IF, COUNTIF and SUMIF let a spreadsheet make decisions.

topics.title: IF: choose between two answers
topics.html:
Formula · IF

=IF(test, answer_if_true, answer_if_false)

The test compares two things with =, >, <, >=, <= or <>. Words in the answers go inside quotation marks.

Comparison signs
SignMeans
=Equal to
>Greater than
<Less than
>=Greater than or equal to
<=Less than or equal to
<>Not equal to
Worked example

Pass or fail

A mark of 40 or more passes. Marks are in B2:B6.

  1. In C2 write =IF(B2>=40,"Pass","Fail").
  2. Copy it down to C6.
  3. 38 gives Fail; 40 gives Pass because the test uses >=.

Answer. The sign you choose decides what happens at the boundary: use >= when exactly 40 should pass.

Watch out

Words inside a formula must be in straight double quotation marks: "Pass". Without them Excel thinks Pass is a name it does not know and shows an error.

Try it yourself: What does =IF(A1>100,"High","Low") show when A1 is 100?

Model answer. It shows Low, because 100 is not greater than 100.

Check what you just learned

1. What does =IF(5>3,"Yes","No") show?
  • Yes (correct)
  • No
  • 5
  • Error

5 is greater than 3, so the test is true.

2. Which sign should you use if exactly 50 must pass?
  • >
  • >= (correct)
  • <
  • <>

>= includes 50.
keyPoints: IF(test, if_true, if_false).
Text answers need quotation marks.
>= includes the boundary value; > does not.

topics.title: Combining tests with AND and OR
topics.html:
Sometimes one test is not enough. AND is true only when all its tests are true. OR is true when at least one is true. You use them inside IF.

AND and OR
FormulaResult for marks 45 and attendance 70
=AND(B2>=40, C2>=75)FALSE (attendance is below 75)
=OR(B2>=40, C2>=75)TRUE (marks are enough)
=IF(AND(B2>=40, C2>=75),"Eligible","Not eligible")Not eligible
Worked example

A scholarship rule

A student needs marks of 60 or more and attendance of 80 or more.

  1. Write =IF(AND(B2>=60,C2>=80),"Yes","No").
  2. A student with 70 marks but 75 attendance gets No.
  3. Changing AND to OR would give Yes.

Answer. Use AND when every rule must be met, OR when any one rule is enough.

Tip

Say the rule out loud first, then write it: 'marks at least 60 AND attendance at least 80'.

Check what you just learned

1. Which function is true only when all its tests are true?
  • OR
  • NOT
  • AND (correct)
  • IF

AND requires every test.

2. =OR(1>2, 3>2) gives:
  • 0
  • FALSE
  • Error
  • TRUE (correct)

The second test is true, which is enough for OR.
keyPoints: AND needs every test true; OR needs one.
Place them inside IF to make a decision.

topics.title: COUNTIF and SUMIF
topics.html:
Formula · COUNTIF

=COUNTIF(range, condition)

Counts the cells in the range that match the condition.

Formula · SUMIF

=SUMIF(range, condition, sum_range)

Adds the cells in sum_range for the rows where range matches the condition.

Conditions you can use
ConditionMeans
"North"Cells equal to the word North
">=40"Numbers 40 or more
"<>Paid"Anything except Paid
E2Whatever is written in cell E2
Worked example

Sales by region

Regions are in A2:A8 and amounts in B2:B8.

  1. =COUNTIF(A2:A8,"North") counts the North rows: 3.
  2. =SUMIF(A2:A8,"North",B2:B8) adds the North amounts: 2350.
  3. Pointing the condition at a cell (E2) lets one formula be copied for every region.

Answer. COUNTIF counts matching rows; SUMIF adds the amounts of matching rows.

Common mistakes

  • Using SUM when only some rows should be added.
  • Making the sum range a different size from the test range.

Check what you just learned

1. Which function adds amounts only for rows that meet a condition?
  • SUMIF (correct)
  • COUNTIF
  • IF
  • AVERAGE

SUMIF adds the rows that match.

2. =COUNTIF(B2:B9,">=50") counts:
  • Cells equal to 50
  • Cells 50 or more (correct)
  • All cells
  • Text cells

>= means 50 or more.

Key terms: flip and sort

IF
Chooses between two answers
Test
A comparison that is true or false
AND
True only when every test is true
OR
True when any test is true
COUNTIF
Counts matching cells
SUMIF
Adds the rows that match
keyPoints: COUNTIF counts matching cells; SUMIF totals matching rows.
A condition can be a word, a comparison in quotes, or a cell.
The test range and the sum range must line up row for row.

modules.title: Organising your data
modules.summary: Keep data in a clean table, then sort and filter it to answer questions.
modules.outcome: You can lay out data so that sorting, filtering and charts work, and you can sort and filter safely.
modules.intro: Most spreadsheet trouble comes from how the data was laid out, not from the formulas. A tidy table makes everything else easy.

topics.title: The rules of a tidy table
topics.html:
Rules of a tidy table

  1. One heading row at the top with a clear name for each column.
  2. One record per row and one kind of information per column.
  3. No blank rows or columns inside the table.
  4. No merged cells inside the data.
  5. Keep totals away from the data, or below it with a gap.
Messy and tidy
MessyTidy
'Pen 10 rs' in one cellItem in one column, price in another
Blank row between monthsNo blank rows
Merged title cells over the dataTitle above, headings directly over the data
January and February in separate small tablesOne table with a Month column
Tip

Think of each table as a list of records, like cards in a box. Every card has the same fields.

Check what you just learned

1. Which breaks a table for sorting?
  • A heading row
  • Bold headings
  • A blank row in the middle (correct)
  • Numbers in column B

Blank rows split the table.

2. What goes in one column of a tidy table?
  • Everything about one person
  • Totals only
  • Several units mixed
  • One kind of information (correct)

Each column holds one kind of information.
keyPoints: One heading row, one record per row, no blank rows or merged cells.
A tidy table makes sorting, filtering and charts work.

topics.title: Sorting without breaking rows
topics.html:
Sorting puts rows in order by one column: smallest to largest, largest to smallest, or A to Z. The golden rule: sort the whole table, not one column. Otherwise names get separated from their numbers.

Worked example

Sorting a race

Times are in B2:B7 and names in A2:A7.

  1. Select the whole table A1:B7, including the headings.
  2. Sort by the Seconds column from smallest to largest.
  3. Each name moves together with its own time: Priya (12.4) rises to the top.

Answer. Select the whole table before sorting so every row moves as one.

Watch out

If you sort only column B, the times are reordered but the names stay where they were. Every name now has the wrong time, and nothing warns you.

Try it yourself: You sort a mark list by marks, largest first. Where does the highest mark appear?

Model answer. In the first row under the heading.

Check what you just learned

1. What is the safest way to sort a table?
  • Select the whole table including its headings (correct)
  • Select one column only
  • Delete the names
  • Sort by colour

Rows must move as complete records.
keyPoints: Sort the whole table so rows stay together.
Ascending is smallest to largest; descending is largest to smallest.

topics.title: Filtering to answer a question
topics.html:
A filter hides the rows that do not match a condition, so you can look at just the ones you care about. The data is not deleted: clearing the filter brings every row back.

Questions a filter can answer
QuestionFilter on
Who passed?Result equals Pass
Which sales were over ₹1,000?Amount greater than 1000
Which orders are from the North?Region equals North

Filtering is for looking; functions such as COUNTIF are for calculating on matching rows. Use a filter to explore, then a formula when you need a number you can reuse.

Tip

After filtering, the row numbers on the left turn blue or skip numbers: that is how you know some rows are hidden.

Check what you just learned

1. What happens to rows hidden by a filter?
  • They are deleted
  • They are only hidden (correct)
  • They turn red
  • They are sorted

Clearing the filter shows them again.

Key terms: flip and sort

Table
Data laid out with headings, one record per row
Record
One row: one customer, order or student
Sort
Put rows in order by a column
Filter
Show only rows that match
Ascending
Smallest to largest, or A to Z
keyPoints: A filter hides non-matching rows without deleting them.
Use filters to look, formulas to calculate.

modules.title: Charts and reports
modules.summary: Turn numbers into charts that answer a question, find and fix errors, and prepare a sheet to share.
modules.outcome: You can pick a suitable chart, build it from a range, read common error messages and share a clean report.
modules.intro: A chart is a sentence in picture form. Done well, it lets a busy reader understand your numbers in five seconds. Done badly, it hides them. This module shows how to choose, build and check.

topics.title: Choosing the right chart
topics.html:
Which chart for which question
Question you are answeringChart
Which category is biggest? How do items compare?Bar (column) chart
How did something change over time?Line chart
What share of a whole does each part take?Pie chart (few parts)
Watch out

A pie chart with more than five slices is hard to read, and a pie only makes sense when the parts add up to a whole.

Tip

Start with the question. If you cannot say what the chart should show in one sentence, do not draw it yet.

Check what you just learned

1. Which chart suits 'how did sales change over twelve months'?
  • Pie
  • Table
  • Line (correct)
  • None

Lines show change over time.

2. When is a pie chart suitable?
  • Negative values
  • Twenty categories
  • Changes over years
  • Showing a share of a whole with a few parts (correct)

Pies show shares of one whole.
keyPoints: Bar to compare, line for change over time, pie for share of a whole.
Choose the chart from the question, not the other way round.

topics.title: Building a clear chart
topics.html:
A chart needs two ranges: labels (the names along the bottom) and values (the numbers). Select a tidy table, choose the chart type, and add the chart.

What makes a chart clear

  • A title that states what it shows.
  • Axis labels or units where they are not obvious.
  • Few colours; one colour for everything unless a bar needs to stand out.
  • Values in a sensible order, for example biggest first.

Common mistakes

  • Charting the totals row together with the data.
  • Leaving the default title, such as Chart 1.
  • Truncating an axis so small differences look huge.

Check what you just learned

1. What two ranges does a bar chart need?
  • Labels and values (correct)
  • Formulas and notes
  • Colours and fonts
  • Rows and sheets

Labels name the bars and values set their height.
keyPoints: A chart uses a labels range and a values range.
Give every chart a title that says what it shows.

topics.title: Errors, checking and sharing
topics.html:
Common error messages
ErrorUsual cause
#DIV/0!Dividing by zero or an empty cell
#VALUE!Doing maths on text
#NAME?A misspelled function or name
#REF!A reference to a cell that no longer exists

Errors are helpful: they say something needs attention. Click the cell, read the formula in the formula bar, and check each cell it points at.

Before you share a sheet

  1. Check that totals match a quick estimate.
  2. Look for error messages and left-aligned numbers.
  3. Delete scratch work or label it clearly.
  4. Name the file clearly and keep a copy of the original.
  5. Export to PDF if you only want people to read it.
Tip

A second pair of eyes finds mistakes you cannot see anymore. Ask a friend to check the totals.

Check what you just learned

1. A cell shows #NAME?. Most likely:
  • Division by zero
  • A misspelled function (correct)
  • A deleted row
  • A date problem

#NAME? means a name the sheet does not know.

2. What is a good last check before sharing?
  • Change colours
  • Add more rows
  • Compare totals with a quick estimate (correct)
  • Hide formulas

A rough estimate reveals gross mistakes.

Key terms: flip and sort

Bar chart
Compares amounts across categories
Line chart
Shows change over time
Pie chart
Shows shares of a whole
Labels
The names along the axis
Values
The numbers the chart draws
keyPoints: Read the error to find the cause.
Check totals against a rough estimate before sharing.
